note: For each domain: the eight steps of the workflow and the performing and ownership conditions for the eight judgment axes. Items, the results report and experience input all read this one file. `verify_targets` and `artifacts` are what the results report's action steps draw on, so they must be concrete here to avoid vague wording

domains.name: Business Strategy and Planning

workflow.name: How the problem arrives
workflow.detail: The work people want to do arrives as a goal or a task

workflow.name: Inputs received
workflow.detail: Company-wide goals, available budget and people, deadline, competitive situation

workflow.name: What gets decided first
workflow.detail: What not to do this time and what to do first

workflow.name: Methods used
workflow.detail: Turning goals into indicators, comparing options, dividing resources, making a schedule

workflow.name: Tools used
workflow.detail: Spreadsheet tools, presentation tools, meeting notes, indicator definition tables

workflow.name: Deliverables produced
workflow.detail: A full business plan, a goals and indicators table, reasons for priorities, an action schedule

workflow.name: What it is compared against
workflow.detail: Company-wide goals, results of past periods, similar cases, achievement rate after the end

workflow.name: When it goes wrong
workflow.detail: If a goal is not achieved, separate whether the goal was too high or resources were not enough

verify_targets: Goals of the whole company or organization
Actual achievement rate after the end

J1.l2: Wrote down the scope to cover this time among the given goals
J1.l3: The scope I defined became the business scope as is

J2.l2: Turned the goal into indicators that measure it with numbers
J2.l3: The indicators I set were used as evaluation criteria

J3.l2: Chose one of several options and allocated resources
J3.l3: The budget or people moved according to the allocation I decided

J4.l2: Chose and used a planning framework or an analysis method
J4.l3: The framework I chose was also used in the next planning

J5.l2: Kept a business plan or plan proposal as a document
J5.l3: Another person read the plan proposal I left and carried it out

J6.l2: Compared two options with the same criteria
J6.l3: Changed the plan based on the comparison results

J7.l2: Narrowed the reason for a missed goal down to the goal or the resources
J7.l3: Confirmed that the same gap became smaller in the next plan

J8.l2: Presented the plan proposal in a meeting, explained it, and received agreement
J8.l3: My plan led to the placement of budget or people

org_outcomes.OC1: A plan that comes back as sales and market share
org_outcomes.OC2: An order plan that fits the needs of a client company
org_outcomes.OC3: A plan that separates profit by channel
org_outcomes.OC4: A business plan that fits the rules and the set forms
org_outcomes.OC5: A project proposal and an execution plan
org_outcomes.OC6: Planning reasons that can show the standards are met
org_outcomes.OC7: A plan that picks what to check before the funds run out

workflow.name: How the problem arrives

workflow.name: Inputs received
workflow.detail: Customer data, records of past responses, available budget, deadline

workflow.name: What gets decided first

domains.name: Financial and Investment Decisions

workflow.name: How the problem arrives
workflow.detail: Work that costs money arrives as something to decide

workflow.name: Inputs received
workflow.detail: Money coming in and going out, available funds, deadline, assumptions such as the discount rate

workflow.name: What gets decided first
workflow.detail: The assumptions for the estimate and the criteria for whether to go ahead

workflow.name: Methods used
workflow.detail: Estimating cash flow, calculating the payback period, checking sensitivity, comparing options

workflow.name: Tools used
workflow.detail: Spreadsheet tools, estimate forms, financial statements, interest rate data

workflow.name: Deliverables produced
workflow.detail: Estimated financial statements, reasons for the investment decision, sensitivity table, funding plan

workflow.name: What it is compared against
workflow.detail: Past results, industry data, the gap between estimate and actual, review comments

workflow.name: When it goes wrong
workflow.detail: If an estimate does not match the results, narrow the reason down to the assumptions or the data

verify_targets: Estimates made with a different method

J1.l2: Wrote down the period and the scope to look at in this decision
J1.l3: The scope I defined became the review scope as is

J2.l2: Turned the goal into criteria such as payback period or profit rate

J3.l2: Decided and wrote down the assumptions for an estimate

J4.l2: Chose and used an estimation method and a calculation framework
J4.l3: The method I chose was also used in the next review

J5.l2: Kept an estimate table and the reasons for the decision as documents

J6.l2: Compared two options with the same criteria
J6.l3: Checked the estimate against actual results and wrote down the gap

J7.l2: Narrowed the reason an estimate was wrong down to the assumptions or the data
J7.l3: Confirmed that the estimate came closer to the results after the assumptions changed

J8.l2: Presented the reasons for the decision in a review or a meeting and explained them
J8.l3: My estimate was used for a budget or investment decision

org_outcomes.OC1: Decisions that come back as operating profit and return on investment
org_outcomes.OC2: Decisions that involve order unit prices and working capital
org_outcomes.OC3: Decisions that involve inventory turnover and channel profit
org_outcomes.OC4: Decisions that are checked by spending rate and audits
org_outcomes.OC5: Decisions made within a project budget
org_outcomes.OC6: Decisions that must pass soundness standards and reviews
org_outcomes.OC7: Decisions viewed by how long it takes until the funds run out

domains.name: Accounting and Cost

workflow.name: How the problem arrives
workflow.detail: Work where money changed hands arrives with its proof

workflow.name: Inputs received
workflow.detail: Proof such as receipts and contracts, the standards that apply, closing deadline

workflow.name: What gets decided first
workflow.detail: Which account to use and which period to put it in

workflow.name: Methods used
workflow.detail: Classifying transactions, recording in the books, checking records against each other, allocating costs, closing adjustments

workflow.name: Tools used
workflow.detail: Accounting software, spreadsheet tools, a storage place for proof, reference standards

workflow.name: Deliverables produced
workflow.detail: Closing data, reconciliation sheet, cost calculation sheet, proof check records

workflow.name: What it is compared against
workflow.detail: Original proof, the standards that apply, numbers of past periods, external review comments

workflow.name: When it goes wrong
workflow.detail: If the numbers do not match, narrow the reason down to classification, period or proof

verify_targets: Values calculated again by another person

J1.l2: Wrote down the range of transactions to cover in this closing

J2.l2: Wrote down the standards that apply and the closing conditions that must be met

J3.l2: Decided which account and which period to use
J3.l3: The classification I decided stayed in the books as is

J5.l2: Kept closing data and a reconciliation sheet as documents
J5.l3: The closing data I left was used in a report or a review

J6.l2: Checked the numbers in the books against the proof one by one
J6.l3: Adjusted the differences found in the check and recorded them

J7.l2: Narrowed the reason the numbers did not match down to classification or period
J7.l3: Changed the recording procedure so that the same error would not happen again

J8.l2: Reported the closing results and received approval
J8.l3: The cost numbers I produced were used in a price or budget decision

org_outcomes.OC2: Closing that separates the cost of each order
org_outcomes.OC3: Closing that separates profit by channel

org_outcomes.OC7: Closing that shows when cash will run out

J1.l2: Wrote down separately the work to move to the system this time and the work to keep
J1.l3: The scope I defined became the introduction scope as is

J2.l2: Turned the spoken requests of the person in charge into a list of tasks
J2.l3: The requirement list I wrote became the basis of the introduction

J3.l2: Decided which work people do and which work the system does
J3.l3: The system was used along the boundary I set

J4.l2: Chose and used a method to draw workflows or compare tools
J4.l3: The method I chose became the team's standard

J5.l2: Kept a workflow diagram and a requirements document as documents
J5.l3: Another person set up or developed the system by reading the document I left

J6.l2: Compared two tools with the same criteria
J6.l3: Checked processing time before and after introduction under the same conditions

J7.l2: Narrowed the reason it is not used down to the requirements or the scope of introduction
J7.l3: Confirmed that it is actually used after the scope changed

J8.l2: Submitted an introduction plan and received approval
J8.l3: The requirement list I wrote became the contract or development scope

review_note: In business majors, roles that produce numbers, roles that check numbers and roles that deal with people sit in one file. What keeps them apart is `required_axes`: planning, human resources, global business and information systems depend on interpreting requirements; operations and customer service depend on failure and correction; finance, accounting, data and demand depend on comparison and verification. So even if six axes are confirmed, the evidence does not hold when a required axis of that domain is empty
